lead: Revelation is the last book of the Bible. A man named John wrote it while exiled on the island of Patmos, probably around AD 95 under the emperor Domitian. Some scholars date it earlier, in the late 60s under Nero, and that date matters a lot for the preterist view.

It is three kinds of writing at once: a letter to seven churches (1:4), a prophecy (1:3), and an apocalypse, a Jewish style of writing that shows heaven's view of earth through symbols. It has 22 chapters and 404 verses. It echoes the Old Testament more than any other New Testament book, yet it never once says "as it is written." Most academic scholars read it first as a message to those churches about Rome in their own day, and some Jewish scholars read it as a Jewish apocalypse by a writer who still saw himself as part of Judaism; Christians have also read it in four main ways, set out on the next page.
facts: John, who calls himself God's slave, his readers' brother, and a fellow slave with the prophets (1:1, 9; 22:9). Tradition: the apostle John. Many scholars: another John, a Jewish-Christian prophet of Asia.
Probably about AD 95, under Domitian (Irenaeus). Some date it to the late 60s, under Nero.
Patmos, an island off the coast of modern Turkey; sent to seven churches of the Roman province of Asia
A letter, a prophecy and an apocalypse at once (1:1–4)

audience.to: Seven real churches in the Roman province of Asia, in what is now western Turkey: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea (1:11). They were small groups of Jewish and Gentile believers meeting in homes in busy, proud cities that honored Rome and the emperor with temples, festivals and statues. John, a prophet they knew, wrote from Patmos, where most think he had been exiled "because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus" (1:9). The book was meant to be read aloud in their gatherings (1:3). Their situations differed. Smyrna was poor, slandered and about to face prison. Philadelphia had little strength and faced the same slander. Pergamum had already lost a martyr, Antipas. Thyatira and Pergamum had teachers who said it was fine to eat at idol feasts. Sardis and Laodicea were comfortable and asleep. Each city's history and trade shows through its letter (chapters 2–3).
audience.why: To show these churches who really rules the world, so they would stay faithful to Jesus whatever it cost. For the pressured churches, the visions are comfort: the slaughtered Lamb has already won, God sees the martyrs, and Babylon will fall. For the comfortable churches, they are a warning. In these cities, many trade and social clubs held meals in honor of a god and the emperor. A Christian who stayed away could lose friends, business and standing. Some Christians ("Jezebel," the Nicolaitans) taught that this kind of compromise was harmless. John answers by showing Rome as a beast and a prostitute drunk on the blood of God's people, and by calling, "Come out of her, my people" (18:4). Knowing the first readers changes the reading. The book is not a puzzle about distant dates written over their heads. It is a pastoral letter that uses the pictures of the prophets to tell seven churches what their own choices meant. However a reader applies it today, it first had to make sense in Ephesus and Laodicea.
views: Some scholars (Ramsay, Hemer) think guild life made refusing very costly, so that a Christian worker had to choose between faith and a living. Others (Harland) think joining a club was voluntary, that many Jews and Christians took part in civic life without trouble, and that John was taking a strict line against Christians who saw no harm in it.

Most scholars follow Irenaeus (about 180), who says John saw the vision near the end of Domitian's reign. The churches' settled state (Ephesus has lost its first love, Laodicea is rich after its rebuilding), the spread of emperor worship in Asia, and the name "Babylon" for Rome, which Jewish writers used after Rome destroyed the Temple in AD 70, fit this date. So does a remark in Polycarp's Letter to the Philippians (11.3) that suggests the church at Smyrna did not yet exist in Paul's day. Some add that the pressure under Domitian came more from local zeal for the emperor than from an empire-wide persecution.

Some scholars date it between 64 and 69, after Nero's killing of Christians in Rome and before the Temple fell. They read the temple that John measures (11:1–2) as still standing, and count the "seven kings" of 17:10 from Julius Caesar or Augustus to land on Nero or Galba. They also argue that Irenaeus's words "it was seen" may refer to John himself, not the vision. Many note that the letters of the name Nero Caesar in Hebrew add up to 666, but many late-date scholars (Bauckham, Aune) accept that too, reading it through the legend that Nero would return, so it is an argument about the beast more than about the date. A few propose the reign of Vespasian (69–79). This date matters most for the Preterist lens, which reads much of the book as fulfilled in the war of AD 66–70.
The first readers were warned about events they would live through: the fall of Jerusalem and the conflict with pagan Rome. The book was mainly for them.
The first readers received the opening of a map of church history that would run from their day to the end. The letters may also stand for ages of the church.

The seven letters were for the first churches (and, for many, for every church), but most of chapters 4–22 describes the last days still to come. The first readers were comforted by knowing how history ends.
The first readers were shown the pattern of every age: the church under pressure from empire and money, and the victory of the Lamb. Their Rome is one face of a power that returns again and again.
Early writers (Tertullian, Clement, Eusebius) say John was exiled there, and most scholars agree. The text says only that he was there "because of the word of God," and a few think he went to preach.

traditions.q: Does Revelation fully belong in the Bible, and should it be read in church worship?
views: It is Scripture, but the East accepted it slowly. Dionysius of Alexandria (about 250) doubted that the apostle wrote it, and Cyril of Jerusalem (about 350) left it off his list of books, as does the list attached to the canons of the Council of Laodicea (canon 60, late 300s, though whether that list is original is debated); to this day it is never read in the Divine Liturgy. Andrew of Caesarea's commentary (about 600–611) became the church's standard guide to it.

Coptic and Ethiopian Bibles include it (the Coptic Church reads the whole book aloud through the night of Holy Saturday, called Apocalypse Night), but others came late. The Armenian Church placed it in its canon only in the Middle Ages, around the 1100s, and the old Syriac Bible (the Peshitta) did not have it; the Syriac Orthodox now accept it, while the separate Assyrian Church of the East has traditionally left it out of its canon.

Yes, without doubt. The West received it early, the councils of Hippo and Carthage (393, 397) list it, Trent (1546) names it the Apocalypse of John the apostle, and it is read at Mass on the Sundays of Easter in one year of the cycle and on the feast of the Assumption.

Received, with a famous early doubt. In 1522 Luther wrote that he missed more than one thing in this book and could hold it neither apostolic nor prophetic; by 1530 he read it more warmly as a picture of church history. In the 1560s Martin Chemnitz still counted it among the once-disputed books. Lutherans today read Revelation 14:6–7 on Reformation Day.

Yes, but the early Reformers kept their distance. Zwingli said it was not a biblical book, and Calvin wrote commentaries on every New Testament book except Revelation and 2–3 John. The Westminster Confession lists it with the rest of the canon.

lenses.name: Preterist
lenses.desc: From Latin praeter, "past." Most of the book was fulfilled in the first centuries: the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 and the conflict with pagan Rome. Partial preterists still expect a future return of Christ (chapters 19–22).

lenses.name: Historicist
lenses.desc: The book is a coded map of church history from John's day to the end. The standard Protestant view from the Reformation to the 1800s (Luther, Isaac Newton, Matthew Henry).

lenses.name: Futurist
lenses.desc: Chapters 4–22 describe events still to come: a tribulation, the Antichrist, Christ's return, and a 1,000-year reign. Most popular American teaching today is a form of this, often dispensational.

lenses.name: Idealist
lenses.desc: A symbolic picture of the battle between God and evil in every age, not a timeline. Its roots go back to Augustine. Many modern scholars mix it with other readings.

Why the Greek texts differ

Revelation survives in fewer manuscripts than any other New Testament book. When Erasmus printed the first Greek New Testament (1516), he had a single incomplete manuscript of Revelation, and he translated its missing last verses back into Greek from the Latin. His later editions corrected some readings from the Complutensian Polyglot, but others, such as "book of life" in 22:19, stayed and passed through the Textus Receptus into the KJV. See .

pages.label: Four ways to read
pages.html:
Before you begin

Four Ways to Read Revelation

Christians have read Revelation four main ways. Each takes the Bible seriously, and each has been held by careful, faithful people. Many readers mix them.

  • PreteristFrom Latin praeter, "past." Most of the book was fulfilled in the first centuries: the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 and the conflict with pagan Rome. Partial preterists still expect a future return of Christ (chapters 19–22).
  • HistoricistThe book is a coded map of church history from John's day to the end. The standard Protestant view from the Reformation to the 1800s (Luther, Isaac Newton, Matthew Henry).
  • FuturistChapters 4–22 describe events still to come: a tribulation, the Antichrist, Christ's return, and a 1,000-year reign. Most popular American teaching today is a form of this, often dispensational.
  • IdealistA symbolic picture of the battle between God and evil in every age, not a timeline. Its roots go back to Augustine. Many modern scholars mix it with other readings.

Most academic scholars, in universities and many seminaries, read Revelation another way, outside the four: as a message to the churches of John's own day about Rome, written in the style of the Jewish apocalypses, with no claim to map out later history. This is called the historical-critical or contemporary-historical reading (Adela Yarbro Collins, David Aune, Steven Friesen, Craig Koester). It shares the preterist view's first-century setting but not its claim that John foretold AD 70. It is the majority view among academic biblical scholars. Futurists and historicists reject it, and many conservative scholars accept its first-century setting while holding that the book also speaks truly of the future. Some Jewish scholars (John W. Marshall, David Frankfurter) read it as a Jewish apocalypse by a writer who still thought of himself as inside Judaism.

Use Lens at the top to highlight one view across every chapter.

Literal or symbolic?

This is not a choice between "taking the Bible seriously" and "not." Every reader takes some parts literally and some as symbol. A futurist reads the sword from Jesus's mouth as a symbol; an idealist believes Jesus literally returns. The real question at each scene is which parts are which.

Where each view places the events

pages.label: Keys to the code
pages.html:
Before you begin

Keys to the Code

How the three sevens fit together

The middle of the book is built from three sets of seven judgments: seals, trumpets and bowls. Readers disagree about how they relate.

One after another: 21 events in a row, common in popular futurism. Nested: the seventh seal opens into the trumpets, and the seventh trumpet into the bowls. Retold: each set covers the same period with growing intensity (a third, then all). This view, called recapitulation, goes back to Victorinus around AD 260, author of the oldest surviving commentary on Revelation. Support for it: the sixth seal already sounds like the end (6:12–17), and the seventh of each set ends with thunder, lightning and an earthquake (8:5; 11:19; 16:18).

The time markers

  • 3½ yearsNamed five ways: 42 months (11:2; 13:5), 1,260 days (11:3; 12:6), "a time, and times, and half a time" (12:14), from Daniel 7:25 and 12:7.
  • 3½ daysThe witnesses lie dead (11:9, 11).
  • 5 monthsThe locusts (9:5, 10).
  • ½ hourSilence in heaven (8:1).
  • 1 hourThe ten kings rule (17:12); Babylon falls (18:10, 17, 19).
  • 10 daysSmyrna's suffering (2:10).
  • 1,000 yearsSatan bound; the saints reign (20:2–7).

Revelation's own decoder

Sometimes the book explains its own symbols. Start here before guessing. When it decodes a symbol, it never decodes it into a date.

  • 1:20The seven stars are the messengers ("angels") of the seven churches.
  • 1:20The seven lampstands are the seven churches.
  • 4:5The seven torches are the seven Spirits of God.
  • 5:6The Lamb’s seven eyes are the seven Spirits sent into all the earth.
  • 5:8The bowls of incense are the prayers of God’s people.
  • 7:14The white robes were washed in the Lamb’s blood.
  • 11:4The two witnesses are the two olive trees and two lampstands.
  • 11:8The great city is "symbolically" Sodom and Egypt, "where their Lord too was crucified."
  • 12:9The dragon is the ancient serpent, the Devil and Satan.
  • 13:18The beast’s number is "the number of a human."
  • 14:4The 144,000 are firstfruits for God and the Lamb.
  • 17:9The seven heads are seven hills, and also seven kings.
  • 17:12The ten horns are ten kings.
  • 17:15The waters are peoples, crowds, nations and languages.
  • 17:18The woman is the great city that rules the kings of the earth.
  • 19:8The fine linen is the righteous acts of God’s people.
  • 19:13The rider’s name is the Word of God.
  • 20:14The lake of fire is the second death.
  • 21:9–10The bride, the Lamb’s wife, is the holy city, New Jerusalem.

pages.label: The beasts
pages.html:
Study page

The Beasts and What They Stand For

Revelation's creatures are built from Old Testament pieces, so the best first clue to any beast is where its parts came from. "Strongest reading" is Claude's judgment of what the text supports best, not a church's or a consensus; the alternatives are given fairly.

The Lamb 5:6

What John sees
Standing, but slaughtered; seven horns, seven eyes
Built from
Isaiah 53:7; Exodus 12
Strongest reading
Jesus, named outright (the Lamb is "the Lord of lords," 17:14). Every beast in the book is a copy of him.
Other readings
None: every view agrees.

Four living creatures 4:6–8

What John sees
Lion, ox, human face, eagle; six wings; full of eyes
Built from
Ezekiel 1; Isaiah 6
Strongest reading
The highest angels, standing for all creation worshiping God. "Full of eyes" means always awake, seeing everything.
Other readings
The four Gospels, though early writers paired them differently: Irenaeus gave John the lion and Mark the eagle; the pairing Christian art made familiar (Matthew the man, Mark the lion, Luke the ox, John the eagle) is Jerome's.

Four horsemen 6:1–8

What John sees
White, red, black and pale-green horses
Built from
Zechariah 1:8; Zechariah 6:1–8
Strongest reading
Conquest, war, famine and death, let loose only as far as they are "given" power.
Other readings
White rider as Christ or the gospel; as the Antichrist; as Parthian archers.

Locusts from the abyss 9:3–11

What John sees
War horses with human faces, crowns, women's hair, lions' teeth, scorpion tails
Built from
Joel 1–2; Exodus 10
Strongest reading
Demonic torment, ruled by "the Destroyer." They cannot touch those with God's seal.
Other readings
Arab armies (historicists); modern aircraft (some futurists); rebel factions and Roman troops (preterists).

The 200 million riders 9:16–19

What John sees
Horses with lion heads, breathing fire, smoke and sulfur
Built from
Ezekiel 38–39
Strongest reading
A demonic army; the number means "beyond counting."
Other readings
A future Asian army; the Ottoman cavalry; the Parthians.

The dragon 12:3–17

What John sees
Red, seven heads with seven crowns, ten horns
Built from
Isaiah 27:1; Psalm 74:13–14 (Leviathan)
Strongest reading
Satan. The text says so outright (12:9). The crowns mean he claims to be king.
Other readings
None: the text names him.

The beast from the sea 13:1–10

What John sees
Leopard body, bear feet, lion mouth; ten crowned horns, seven heads, one wounded and healed
Built from
Daniel 7:1–8
Strongest reading
Political power that demands worship. Its first target is Rome. Futurists add a final world ruler.
Other readings
Nero (preterists); the papacy (Reformers); a future Antichrist (futurists).

The beast from the earth 13:11–17

What John sees
Two horns like a lamb, speaks like a dragon; later called "the false prophet" (16:13; 19:20)
Built from
Deuteronomy 13:1–3
Strongest reading
Religion and propaganda that serve the state, like the priests of the emperor's cult in Asia.
Other readings
A future religious leader; the papal hierarchy; Jewish leaders who cooperated with Rome.

The scarlet beast 17:3–14

What John sees
Scarlet, covered in insulting names; seven heads, ten horns; ridden by a woman
Built from
Daniel 7:7, 24
Strongest reading
The same beast in its final form. It "was, and is not, and is about to come up," a parody of God, "who is, who was, and who is coming" (1:4).
Other readings
The legend that Nero would return; a revived Roman Empire.

The prostitute 17:1–6

What John sees
Dressed in purple and scarlet, gold cup, seated on many waters
Built from
Ezekiel 16; Jeremiah 51
Strongest reading
"The great city that holds royal power over the kings of the earth" (17:18): the seduction of wealth and false worship.
Other readings
Rome; Jerusalem; a false church; a future global economy.

The pattern behind them

Every evil figure in Revelation is a cheap copy of something holy. The dragon, the beast and the false prophet imitate the Father, the Son and the Spirit (16:13). The beast has a death-wound "as slaughtered," like the Lamb (13:3; 5:6). The land beast has horns "like a lamb" (13:11). The beast "was, and is not, and is about to come up," mocking God, "who is, who was, and who is coming" (17:8; 1:4). The mark on the forehead copies God's seal (13:16; 7:3). A reader who learns to spot the counterfeit is doing what 13:18 asks: "Here is where wisdom comes in."

pages.label: Church and Israel
pages.html:
Study page

The Church and the Nation of Israel

Does Revelation see one people of God or two? The question shapes how you read chapters 7, 11, 12, 14, 20 and 21.

For two distinct peoples

  • "Church" appears 19 times in chapters 1–3, then not again until 22:16.
  • The 144,000 are listed tribe by tribe (7:4–8).
  • Jerusalem is central: "where their Lord too was crucified" (11:8), "the beloved city" (20:9).
  • The woman of chapter 12 matches Joseph's dream of Israel (Genesis 37:9).
  • Paul expects a future turning of Israel (Romans 11:25–26).

For one people

  • The church is called a "kingdom and priests" (1:6; 5:10), Israel's title from Exodus 19:6.
  • "Those who say they are Jews and are not" (2:9; 3:9).
  • John hears 144,000 from Israel and sees a crowd from every nation (7:4, 9).
  • One bride (19:7). One city, with Israel's tribes on the gates and the apostles on the foundations (21:12–14).
  • Paul: those who belong to Christ are Abraham's offspring and heirs of the promise (Galatians 3:29).

The main positions

Dispensational

Israel and church
Two peoples with two sets of promises. The church is raptured before the tribulation, and God then deals with national Israel.
Reading Revelation
Chapters 6–19 are Daniel’s 70th week for Israel. The 144,000 are Jewish. The millennium fulfills Israel’s land promises.

Progressive dispensational

Israel and church
One people of God in Christ, but ethnic Israel keeps a real future role.
Reading Revelation
A similar timeline, with more overlap between Israel and the church.

Historic premillennial

Israel and church
One people, plus a future mass turning of Jews to Jesus (Romans 11).
Reading Revelation
The church goes through the tribulation; Christ then reigns 1,000 years.

Covenant (amil or postmil)

Israel and church
One people. The church continues and fulfills Israel, and Jewish believers remain part of it.
Reading Revelation
The 144,000 and the crowd are the same people. The new Jerusalem is the whole church.

Preterist

Israel and church
Varies. The focus is judgment on first-century Jerusalem’s leaders, not on the Jewish people.
Reading Revelation
Babylon may be Jerusalem in AD 70. This has been misused to fuel hostility toward Jews, which careful preterists firmly reject.

Messianic Jewish

Israel and church
One body in Messiah, in which Jewish believers keep their Jewish identity and calling.
Reading Revelation
Reads the tribal names and Jerusalem as lasting signs of God’s faithfulness to Israel.
Claude’s theory my own idea, not established scholarship
One tree, with Israel at its root

Revelation never "replaces" Israel. It names the tribes one by one and writes them on the gates of the final city. But it also never keeps two separate peoples in its final picture: one bride, one city, one Lamb. My reading is closest to Paul's single olive tree in Romans 11, where Israel is the trunk and the nations are grafted in. The tribe names on the gates say "you enter through Israel," and the apostles on the foundations say "you stand on the gospel."

Romans 11:17–24; Revelation 21:12–14; Revelation 19:7

Notes in the text

  • 1:18 · Greek religion gave these keys to Hecate or Aeacus. Jewish teachers gave them to God alone.

  • 12:1 · Goddesses were pictured crowned with stars. So was the European flag.

  • 12:3 · Canaanite texts describe Litan, "the mighty one with seven heads."

  • 12:5 · In Greek myth a dragon hunted a pregnant goddess. Ephesus told this story.

Art and Image Prompts

Every drawing on this scroll is an original sketch made for this page, so it needs no credit or license. The map is drawn from the cities' real locations.

Public domain art to look at

  • Albrecht Dürer, The Apocalypse (1498)

    Fifteen woodcuts, including the Four Horsemen and the Woman and the Dragon. Public domain.

  • Bamberg Apocalypse (Reichenau, about 1000–1020)

    Illuminated manuscript with bright, flat figures. Public domain.

  • Facundus Beatus (Spain, 1047)

    A copy of Beatus of Liébana’s commentary, with bold Mozarabic paintings of the beasts. Public domain.

  • The Cloisters Apocalypse (Normandy, about 1330)

    Held by the Metropolitan Museum; its photos are released under Open Access (CC0).

  • The Apocalypse Tapestry (Angers, 1377–1382)

    The largest medieval tapestry series. The work is public domain; check each photo’s license.

  • William Blake, The Great Red Dragon paintings (1805–1810)

    Four watercolors of Revelation 12. Public domain.

prompts: One like a son of man (1:12–16)

A tall figure in a long robe reaching to the feet with a gold sash across the chest; hair white as wool; eyes like flames; feet glowing like bronze in a furnace; face shining like the sun; a sharp two-edged sword coming from his mouth; seven stars held in his right hand; seven separate gold oil lampstands standing around him; the apostle John fallen at his feet on a rocky island shore.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, Egyptian hieroglyphic register lines and small glyph borders, plus a few bold flat shapes of lapis blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp corners, no lettering. Wide horizontal composition, 3:2.

reading: Steve Gregg, Revelation: Four Views (rev. ed. 2013)
Prints preterist, historicist, futurist and idealist commentary side by side, verse by verse. The best single tool for comparing the views fairly.
Richard Bauckham, The Theology of the Book of Revelation (1993)
Short and readable. The source for many of the patterns noted here, such as the 28 uses of "Lamb" for Christ.
Craig Keener, Revelation (NIV Application Commentary, 2000)
Clear, practical and fair to all the views.
Michael Gorman, Reading Revelation Responsibly (2011)
A short guide to reading Revelation as a call to faithful witness.
G. K. Beale, The Book of Revelation (NIGTC, 1999)
A large Greek-based commentary, strong on Old Testament background. Idealist with future fulfillment.
Craig Koester, Revelation (Anchor Yale Bible, 2014)
A major scholarly commentary, rich in Roman-world history.
David Aune, Revelation (Word Biblical Commentary, 3 vols., 1997–98)
The most detailed technical commentary, with ancient parallels.
John Walvoord, The Revelation of Jesus Christ (1966; updated 2011)
The classic dispensational futurist commentary.
Robert L. Thomas, Revelation 1–7 and Revelation 8–22 (1992–95)
A detailed literal, futurist reading of the Greek text.
Kenneth Gentry, Before Jerusalem Fell (1989)
The main case for dating Revelation before AD 70, the basis of preterism.
Adela Yarbro Collins, The Combat Myth in the Book of Revelation (1976)
The study of Revelation 12 and the ancient dragon myths.
Bruce Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament (2nd ed. 1994)
Explains each manuscript difference, including 13:18, 22:14 and 22:19.
